approach: Find the time when the applied force reaches the maximum static friction, then use kinetic friction for the sliding phase after that time.

steps.text: Find the maximum static friction and the time at which the applied force reaches it.
steps.equation: f(max static) = μₛmg = 0.6×2×10 = 12 N; F = 2t = 12 N at t = 6 s

steps.text: For t < 6 s the block stays still, so friction equals the applied force.
For t > 6 s the block slides, so kinetic friction takes its constant value and the net force gives the acceleration.
At t = 2 s the block is still in the static phase.
At t = 8 s the block is in the sliding phase.

final_answer.value: (a) a = 0 for 0 ≤ t ≤ 6 s, then a = t − 4 for t > 6 s, a straight line starting at (6 s, 2 m/s²) with slope 1; (b) friction = 4 N at t = 2 s, friction = 8 N at t = 8 s

common_mistakes.text: Using the static coefficient 0.6 instead of the kinetic coefficient 0.4 for the sliding phase gives friction = 12 N at t = 8 s and a = 2 m/s² instead of 4 m/s².
Forgetting to divide the net force by the mass gives a = 2t − 8 directly, so a = 8 m/s² at t = 8 s instead of the correct 4 m/s².
